translations.literal: Liu was displeased and secretly sent Can to kill him.
translations.idiomatic: Liu took offense and secretly ordered Shen Can to murder him.

sentences.zh: 始，孺休見攻也，曰：「勿殺我，當與爾金。」

translations.literal: When Ru-Xiu was first attacked, he said, "Do not kill me—I will give you gold."
translations.idiomatic: As the attack began Ru-Xiu cried, "Do not kill me—I will give you gold."

sentences.zh: 粲曰：「殺爾，金焉往？」

translations.literal: Can said, "If I kill you, where will the gold go?"
translations.idiomatic: Can replied, "Kill you, and where will the gold go?"

sentences.zh: 與兄述休同死。

translations.literal: He and his elder brother Shu-Xiu died together.
translations.idiomatic: He and his elder brother Shu-Xiu perished together.

sentences.zh: 悰弟 慆悰弟慆。

translations.literal: Cong's younger brother Tao. Tao.
translations.idiomatic: Cong's younger brother Tao.

sentences.zh: 慆，咸通中為泗州刺史。

translations.literal: Tao, in the Xiantong era, was prefect of Sizhou.
translations.idiomatic: During the Xiantong period Tao served as prefect of Sizhou.

sentences.zh: 會龐勛反，圍城，處士辛讜自廣陵來見慆，勸出家屬，獨以身守。

translations.literal: When Pang Xun rebelled and besieged the city, the retired scholar Xin Dan came from Guangling to see Tao and urged him to send his family away and guard the city alone.
translations.idiomatic: When Pang Xun rose in rebellion and laid siege to the city, the recluse Xin Dan came from Guangling and advised Tao to evacuate his household and defend the walls himself.

sentences.zh: 慆曰：「吾出百口求生，眾心搖矣，不如與將士生死共之。」

translations.literal: Tao said, "If I lead a hundred mouths out to save our lives, the hearts of the multitude will waver; better to live and die with the officers and soldiers."
translations.idiomatic: Tao said, "If I march a hundred dependents out to safety, the garrison's heart will break. I would rather stand or fall with the troops."

sentences.zh: 眾聞皆泣下。

translations.literal: On hearing this, all wept.
translations.idiomatic: At those words the defenders wept.

sentences.zh: 慆之聞難，完濬城隍，閱器械無不具。

translations.literal: When Tao heard of the crisis, he had repaired the walls and moats and inspected weapons—nothing was lacking.
translations.idiomatic: As soon as word of the uprising reached him, Tao had strengthened walls and moats and inventoried arms until nothing was wanting.

sentences.zh: 賊將李圓易慆，馳勇士百人欲入封府庫，慆為好言厚禮迎勞，賊不虞慆之謀也。

translations.literal: The rebel general Li Yuan looked down on Tao; he galloped a hundred braves intending to enter and seal the treasury, but Tao welcomed them with fair words and generous gifts, and the rebels did not suspect Tao's design.
translations.idiomatic: Rebel commander Li Yuan despised Tao and sent a hundred picked men at full gallop to seize the treasury. Tao received them with smooth speech and rich gifts, and they never guessed his intent.

sentences.zh: 明日，伏甲士三百，宴球場，賊皆殲焉。

translations.literal: The next day he hid three hundred armored men and held a feast on the ball ground; the rebels were all destroyed.
translations.idiomatic: The next day he hid three hundred armored men and gave a feast on the drill field. Every rebel in the trap was killed.

sentences.zh: 圓怒，傅城戰，慆殺數百人，圓退壁城西。

translations.literal: Yuan was enraged and pressed the siege; Tao killed several hundred men, and Yuan withdrew to fortify west of the city.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan flew into a rage and assaulted the walls. Tao cut down hundreds of attackers and Yuan pulled back to entrench west of the city.

sentences.zh: 勛聞，益其兵，而以書射城中促降。

translations.literal: When Xun heard, he reinforced the army and shot a letter into the city urging surrender.
translations.idiomatic: Pang Xun, hearing of it, sent more troops and shot a letter into the city demanding capitulation.

sentences.zh: 會夜，慆擊鼓乘城大呼，圓氣奪，奔還徐州。

translations.literal: One night Tao beat the drums, mounted the wall, and shouted; Yuan's spirit was broken and he fled back to Xuzhou.
translations.idiomatic: One night Tao beat the drums, climbed the ramparts, and roared defiance until Yuan's nerve broke and he retreated to Xuzhou.

sentences.zh: 未幾，賊焚淮口，晝夜戰不息，讜乃請救於戍將郭厚本，賊解去。

translations.literal: Before long the rebels burned the Huai River mouth; day and night the fighting did not cease, and Dan then asked relief from the garrison commander Guo Houben, and the rebels withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: Soon the rebels torched the Huai estuary and battle raged without pause. Xin Dan appealed to garrison commander Guo Houben for aid, and the besiegers drew off.

sentences.zh: 浙西節度使杜審權遣將以兵千人來援，反為圓軍所包，一軍盡沒。

translations.literal: The Zhexi military commissioner Du Shenquan dispatched a general with a thousand men to aid them, but they were in turn surrounded by Yuan's army and the whole force perished.
translations.idiomatic: Zhexi commissioner Du Shenquan sent a general with a thousand men to relieve the city, but Yuan's troops enveloped them and the entire detachment was wiped out.

sentences.zh: 慆使人間道走京師，詔戴可師以沙陀、吐渾兵二萬招討。

translations.literal: Tao sent a man by a hidden route to the capital; an edict appointed Dai Keshi to recruit and suppress with twenty thousand Shatuo and Togon troops.
translations.idiomatic: Tao sent a messenger by secret paths to the capital. The court ordered Dai Keshi to take the field with twenty thousand Shatuo and Togon horsemen.

sentences.zh: 淮南節度使令狐遣牙將李湘屯淮口，與郭厚本合，為圓所敗，湘等並沒，於是援絕。

translations.literal: The Huainan military commissioner Linghu sent his adjutant Li Xiang to garrison the Huai mouth and join Guo Houben, but they were defeated by Yuan; Xiang and the rest all perished, and relief was cut off.
translations.idiomatic: Huainan commissioner Linghu Chu dispatched adjutant Li Xiang to hold the Huai estuary alongside Guo Houben. Yuan routed them; Xiang and his men were lost, and outside help ceased.

sentences.zh: 賊乃以鐵鎖絕淮流，梯沖乘城。

translations.literal: The rebels then stretched iron chains across the Huai current and brought scaling ladders and assault towers against the walls.
translations.idiomatic: The rebels then spanned the Huai with iron chains and brought up scaling ladders and assault towers against the walls.

sentences.zh: 糧盡，為薄饘以給。

translations.literal: When grain was exhausted, they issued thin gruel for rations.
translations.idiomatic: When stores ran out they fed the garrison thin gruel.

sentences.zh: 懿宗遣使加慆檢校右散騎常侍，勉以堅守。

translations.literal: Emperor Yizong sent envoys to add to Tao the acting post of Right Regular Attendant and to encourage steadfast defense.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Yizong sent envoys to grant Tao the acting rank of Right Regular Attendant and to urge him to hold fast.

sentences.zh: 勛遣圓入城見慆約降，慆怒殺之。

translations.literal: Xun sent Yuan into the city to see Tao and negotiate surrender; Tao in anger killed him.
translations.idiomatic: Xun sent Yuan into the city to treat for surrender. Tao, enraged, had him executed.

sentences.zh: 勛復遺之書，答書言安祿山、朱泚等終底覆滅者，以陰攜其黨。

translations.literal: Xun again sent him a letter; the reply cited how An Lushan, Zhu Ci, and the like in the end were utterly destroyed, to secretly shake his faction.
translations.idiomatic: Xun wrote again. Tao's answer reminded him how An Lushan, Zhu Ci, and such rebels had ended in total ruin—a message meant to unsettle the rebel ranks.

sentences.zh: 勛累攻不得志，會招討使馬舉率兵至，遂解去。

translations.literal: Xun repeatedly attacked without success; when the pacification commissioner Ma Ju led troops up, they at last lifted the siege and departed.
translations.idiomatic: Pang Xun assaulted the city again and again without gain. When pacification commissioner Ma Ju arrived with his army, the rebels finally broke off the siege and withdrew.

sentences.zh: 圍凡十月，慆拊循士，皆殊死奮，而辛讜冒圍出入，糾輯援師，卒完一州，時稱為難。

translations.literal: The siege lasted ten months in all; Tao comforted and led the troops, who all fought to the death, while Xin Dan braved the encirclement in and out, gathered relief forces, and in the end preserved the whole prefecture—at the time it was called a feat amid hardship.
translations.idiomatic: The siege ran ten months. Tao rallied his men until they fought as if death meant nothing, while Xin Dan slipped through the lines again and again to marshal relief. In the end the prefecture stood intact—men called it a triumph born of ordeal.

sentences.zh: 賊平，慆遷義成軍節度使，檢校兵部尚書，卒。

translations.literal: When the rebels were pacified, Tao was transferred as military commissioner of Yicheng, made acting Minister of War, and died in office.
translations.idiomatic: After the rebellion was crushed Tao was made military commissioner of Yicheng and acting Minister of War, and died in that post.

sentences.zh: 從郁子 牧牧，字牧之，善屬文。

translations.literal: Of Tao's issue by the concubine Yu: Mu. Mu, courtesy name Muzhi, was skilled at literary composition.
translations.idiomatic: Tao's son by the concubine Yu was Mu, styled Muzhi, a master of literary composition.

sentences.zh: 第進士，復舉賢良方正。

translations.literal: He passed the jinshi examination and again was chosen in the "excellent and upright" category.
translations.idiomatic: He took the jinshi degree and was later selected in the "excellent and upright" civil-service examination.

sentences.zh: 沈傳師表為江西團練府巡官，又為牛僧孺淮南節度府掌書記。

translations.literal: Shen Chuanshi recommended him as circuit patrol officer of Jiangxi, and again he served as secretarial aide in Niu Sengru's Huainan headquarters.
translations.idiomatic: Shen Chuanshi recommended him as Jiangxi circuit patrol officer, and he later served as secretarial aide on Niu Sengru's Huainan staff.

sentences.zh: 擢監察御史，移疾分司東都，以弟顗病棄官。

translations.literal: He was promoted to investigating censor, then pleaded illness and took a post in the eastern capital without portfolio, abandoning office because his younger brother Yi was ill.
translations.idiomatic: Promoted to investigating censor, he soon pleaded illness and withdrew to a nominal post in the eastern capital to nurse his younger brother Yi.

sentences.zh: 復為宣州團練判官，拜殿中侍御史內供奉。

translations.literal: He again became aide of the Xuancheng training commission and was appointed Palace Attendant within the Inner Service.
translations.idiomatic: He returned as aide on the Xuancheng training commission and was named Palace Attendant in the inner service.

sentences.zh: 是時，劉從諫守澤潞，何進滔據魏博，頗驕蹇不循法度。

translations.literal: At that time Liu Congjian held Zelu, and He Jintao held Weibo; both were quite arrogant and did not follow the laws.
translations.idiomatic: At that time Liu Congjian held Zelu and He Jintao held Weibo; both were proud and scorned imperial law.

sentences.zh: 牧追咎長慶以來朝廷措置亡術，復失山東，鉅封劇鎮，所以系天下輕重，不得承襲輕授，皆國家大事，嫌不當位而言，實有罪，故作《罪言》。

translations.literal: Mu traced the blame to the court's inept measures since the Changqing era, when Shandong was again lost; the great, strategic circuits that bind the weight of the realm must not be lightly inherited or lightly appointed—all matters of state. Though his rank made speech improper, he was in truth guilty, and so he wrote "Words of Guilt."
translations.idiomatic: Du Mu traced the ruin to court blunders since the Changqing years and the renewed loss of the Shandong heartland. The great frontier circuits that anchor the empire's balance, he argued, must never pass by casual inheritance or casual appointment. Though his office made such speech improper, he felt himself guilty of silence and composed "Words of Guilt."

sentences.zh: 其辭曰：

translations.literal: Its text says:
translations.idiomatic: The essay reads:

sentences.zh: 生人常病兵，兵祖於山東，羨於天下。

translations.literal: The living constantly suffer from warfare; warfare takes its origin in Shandong and is envied by the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Mortals are forever sick with war. War is born in Shandong and coveted by all under Heaven.

sentences.zh: 不得山東，兵不可去。

translations.literal: Without Shandong, warfare cannot depart.
translations.idiomatic: Without Shandong, war will not leave the realm.

sentences.zh: 山東之地，禹畫九土曰冀州；

translations.literal: The land of Shandong—in Yu's delineation of the nine provinces it was Jizhou;
translations.idiomatic: The Shandong region: in Yu's partition of the nine provinces it was Jizhou;

sentences.zh: 舜以其分太大，離為幽州，為并州。

translations.literal: Shun, because its share was too large, divided off Youzhou and Bingzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Shun, finding its territory too vast, split off Youzhou and Bingzhou.

sentences.zh: 程其水土，與河南等，常重十二，故其人沈鷙多材力，重許可，能辛苦。

translations.literal: Measuring its soil and water against Henan and the rest, it commonly weighed twelve parts heavier; hence its people were deep and fierce, rich in strength, heavy on promises, able to endure hardship.
translations.idiomatic: Measured against the central plain, its soil and water ranked a full twelve parts heavier in martial virtue. Its people were grave, fierce, and strong; they prized their word and could bear hardship.

sentences.zh: 魏晉以下，工機纖雜，意態百出，俗益卑弊，人益脆弱，唯山東敦五種，本兵矢，他不能蕩而自若也。

translations.literal: From Wei and Jin downward, craft grew intricate and subtle, manners ever more base, people ever more frail; only Shandong kept to the five grains and the root of arms and arrows, and nothing else could sweep it away—it held itself as before.
translations.idiomatic: From Wei and Jin onward the world turned to fine contrivance and shifting fashion; manners sank and constitutions weakened. Only Shandong clung to the five grains and the source of bow and blade. Nothing could wash it away; it remained itself.

sentences.zh: 產健馬，下者日馳二百里，所以兵常當天下。

translations.literal: It produces strong horses; the inferior ones still run two hundred li a day—hence its soldiery constantly matched the realm.
translations.idiomatic: It breeds war-horses; even the poor stock gallops two hundred li in a day. That is why its armies have always matched the empire.

sentences.zh: 冀州，以其恃強不循理，冀其必破弱；

translations.literal: Jizhou—because it relied on strength and did not follow reason, one hoped it would surely be broken and weakened;
translations.idiomatic: Jizhou: because it trusts in force and scorns principle, men wished it broken and humbled;

sentences.zh: 雖已破，冀其復強大也。

translations.literal: though already broken, one still hoped it would again grow strong.
translations.idiomatic: yet even when broken they still feared it would rise strong again.

sentences.zh: 并州，力足以並吞也。

translations.literal: Bingzhou—strength enough to swallow in union.
translations.idiomatic: Bingzhou: power enough to swallow rivals whole.

sentences.zh: 幽州，幽陰慘殺也。

translations.literal: Youzhou—gloom, yin, cruelty, and slaughter.
translations.idiomatic: Youzhou: shadow, chill, cruelty, and killing.

sentences.zh: 聖人因以為名。

translations.literal: The sages therefore took these as names.
translations.idiomatic: The sages named the provinces from these very qualities.

sentences.zh: 黃帝時，蚩尤為兵階，自後帝王多居其地。

translations.literal: In the time of the Yellow Emperor, Chiyou was the stair of warfare; afterward emperors and kings mostly dwelt in that land.
translations.idiomatic: In the age of the Yellow Emperor, Chiyou was the threshold of war. Afterward emperors and kings made their seat there again and again.

sentences.zh: 周劣齊霸，不一世，晉大，常傭役諸侯。

translations.literal: Zhou was weak and Qi hegemonic, not lasting one generation; Jin grew great and constantly pressed the feudal lords into service.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou waned while Qi held hegemony for a single generation; Jin grew mighty and constantly drafted the feudal lords to its wars.

sentences.zh: 至秦萃銳三晉，經六世乃能得韓，遂折天下脊；

translations.literal: When Qin gathered the sharp edge of the Three Jins, through six reigns it was only then able to take Han and so break the spine of the realm;
translations.idiomatic: Qin honed the Three Jins' keen edge; only after six reigns could it seize Han and snap the backbone of the empire;

sentences.zh: 復得趙，因拾取諸國。

translations.literal: it again took Zhao and thereby picked up the other states.
translations.idiomatic: then took Zhao and gathered the rest of the realm in its hand.

sentences.zh: 韓信聯齊有之，故蒯通知漢、楚輕重在信。

translations.literal: When Han Xin joined Qi and held it, Kuai Tong therefore told Han and Chu that the weight of the realm lay with Xin.
translations.idiomatic: When Han Xin held Qi, Kuai Tong told the contending courts that the balance of empire rested on him alone.

sentences.zh: 光武始於上谷，成於鄗。

translations.literal: Guangwu began at Shanggu and was completed at Hao.
translations.idiomatic: Guangwu rose from Shanggu and finished his work at Hao.

sentences.zh: 魏武舉官渡，三分天下有其二。

translations.literal: Cao Wu raised troops at Guandu and held two parts of the realm in three.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao fought at Guandu and came to hold two thirds of the world.

sentences.zh: 晉亂胡作，至宋武號英雄，得蜀，得關中，盡有河南地，十分天下之八，然不能使一人度河以窺胡。

translations.literal: When Jin was thrown into disorder the barbarians rose; down to Emperor Wu of Song, styled a hero, he gained Shu, gained Guanzhong, and fully held the lands of Henan—eight tenths of the realm—yet could not make a single man cross the river to spy on the Hu.
translations.idiomatic: Jin's collapse let the northern tribes in. Even Emperor Wu of Song, hailed as a hero, won Shu and Guanzhong and held eight tenths of Henan—eight tenths of the realm—yet could not send one man across the river to probe the barbarians.

sentences.zh: 至高齊荒蕩，宇文取之，隋文因以滅陳，五百年間，天下乃一家。

translations.literal: When the Northern Qi fell to wild ruin, the Yuwen took it; Sui Wen thereby destroyed Chen, and within five hundred years the realm became one household.
translations.idiomatic: When Northern Qi collapsed into chaos the Yuwen seized it; Sui Wen used that base to destroy Chen, and within five hundred years the realm was one house again.

sentences.zh: 隋文非宋武敵也，是宋不得山東，隋得山東，故隋為王，宋為霸。

translations.literal: Sui Wen was no match for Song Wu; it was that Song did not gain Shandong while Sui gained Shandong—hence Sui became king and Song remained hegemon.
translations.idiomatic: Sui Wendi was no equal to Song Wu-di; but Song lacked Shandong while Sui held it. That is why Sui ruled as king and Song only as hegemon.

sentences.zh: 由此言之，山東，王者不得不為王，霸者不得不為霸，猾賊得之，足以致天下不安。

translations.literal: From this speaking, Shandong—a true king must have it to be king, a hegemon must have it to be hegemon; if a cunning bandit obtains it, he is enough to throw the realm into unrest.
translations.idiomatic: So viewed: Shandong is ground a true king cannot reign without, a hegemon cannot dominate without. Let a cunning outlaw take it, and the realm will not know peace.

sentences.zh: 天寶末，燕盜起，出入成臯、函、潼間，若涉無人地。

translations.literal: At the end of the Tianbao era, the Yan bandits rose, going in and out among Chenggao, Hangu, and Tong—like treading land without a man.
translations.idiomatic: At the close of Tianbao the Yan rebels rose and moved through Chenggao, Hangu, and Tong as if no one stood on the earth.

sentences.zh: 郭、李輩兵五十萬，不能過鄴。

translations.literal: Guo, Li, and their kind with five hundred thousand troops could not pass Ye.
translations.idiomatic: Guo Ziyi, Li Guangbi, and their hosts—five hundred thousand strong—could not break through at Ye.

sentences.zh: 自爾百餘城，天下力盡，不得尺寸，人望之若回鶻、吐蕃，義無敢窺者。

translations.literal: From then more than a hundred cities; the realm's strength was spent and could not gain an inch; men looked on them as on the Uyghurs and Tibetans—righteousness had none who dared peer in.
translations.idiomatic: After that a hundred-odd cities stood beyond reach. The empire exhausted its strength and won not a span of ground. Men gazed on the rebels as they did on Uyghur and Tibetan hosts—no one dared even look their way.

sentences.zh: 國家因之畦河修障戍，塞其街蹊。

translations.literal: The state therefore partitioned the Yellow River, repaired barrier forts, and blocked their streets and paths.
translations.idiomatic: The court walled off the Yellow River, rebuilt frontier posts, and choked every road they might use.

sentences.zh: 齊、魯、梁、蔡被其風流，因以為寇。

translations.literal: Qi, Lu, Liang, and Cai caught their drift and in turn became marauders.
translations.idiomatic: Qi, Lu, Liang, and Cai caught the contagion and turned raider in their turn.

sentences.zh: 以裏拓表，以表撐裏，混澒回轉，顛倒橫邪，未常五年間不戰。

translations.literal: Using the inner to stretch the outer, using the outer to prop the inner, churning and revolving in confusion, inverted and askew—never five years without battle.
translations.idiomatic: Heartland propped frontier, frontier propped heartland; the realm churned and spun, upside down and awry—scarcely five years passed without war.

sentences.zh: 生人日頓委，四夷日日熾，天子因之幸陜，幸漢中，焦焦然七十餘年。

translations.literal: The living daily dwindled; the four barbarians daily grew fierce; the Son of Heaven therefore sojourned at Shaan and Hanzhong, anxious and harried for more than seventy years.
translations.idiomatic: The people wasted day by day; the border peoples waxed day by day. Emperors fled to Shaan and Hanzhong, harried and worn, for more than seventy years.

sentences.zh: 運遭孝武，澣衣一肉，不畋不樂，自卑冗中拔取將相，凡十三年，乃能盡得河南、山西地，洗削更革，罔不能適。

translations.literal: Fortune met Emperor Xiaowu; he washed his robes to a single layer of cloth and a single dish of meat, did not hunt and did not take pleasure, raised generals and ministers from humble ranks—for thirteen years he was able fully to regain the lands of Henan and Shanxi, scour and reform, and nothing could fail to suit.
translations.idiomatic: Fate brought Emperor Xiaowu of Tang. He wore one robe, ate one dish, hunted no more and feasted no more, and plucked generals and ministers from the humble ranks. In thirteen years he recovered Henan and Shanxi, scoured the realm clean, and bent every part to his will.

sentences.zh: 唯山東不服，亦再攻之，皆不利。

translations.literal: Only Shandong did not submit; he attacked it twice, both times without advantage.
translations.idiomatic: Only Shandong would not bow. He struck it twice and failed both times.

sentences.zh: 豈天使生人未至於怗泰邪？

translations.literal: Was it Heaven's intent that the living had not yet reached settled peace?
translations.idiomatic: Had Heaven decreed that the people were not yet due for peace?

sentences.zh: 豈人謀未至邪？

translations.literal: Had human counsel not yet arrived?
translations.idiomatic: Had human wisdom not yet found its hour?

sentences.zh: 何其艱哉！

translations.literal: How arduous it was!
translations.idiomatic: How bitter the road was!

sentences.zh: 今日天子聖明，超出古昔，誌於平治。

translations.literal: Today the Son of Heaven is sagely and bright, surpassing the ancients, with will set on great peace.
translations.idiomatic: Today's emperor is sage and luminous, exceeding the ancients, his heart set on universal order.

sentences.zh: 若欲悉使生人無事，其要先去兵。

translations.literal: If one wishes fully to make the living without affair, the first thing is to remove warfare.
translations.idiomatic: If he would truly free the people from care, he must first drive war away.

sentences.zh: 不得山東，兵不可去。

translations.literal: Without Shandong, warfare cannot depart.
translations.idiomatic: Without Shandong, war will not leave the realm.

sentences.zh: 今者，上策莫如自治。

translations.literal: At present, the highest policy is nothing but self-governance.
translations.idiomatic: At present the supreme strategy is to govern the realm aright.

sentences.zh: 何者？

translations.literal: How so?
translations.idiomatic: How so?

sentences.zh: 當貞元時，山東有燕、趙、魏叛，河南有齊、蔡叛，梁、徐、陳、汝、白馬津、盟津、襄、鄧、安、黃、壽春皆戍厚兵十餘所，才足自護治所，實不輟一人以他使，遂使我力解勢弛，熟視不軌者無可奈何。

translations.literal: In the Zhenyuan era, Shandong had Yan, Zhao, and Wei in rebellion; Henan had Qi and Cai in rebellion; Liang, Xu, Chen, Ru, Baima Ford, Meng Ford, Xiang, Deng, An, Huang, and Shouchun all had thick garrisons of more than ten posts—barely enough to guard their own seats of government, in truth not releasing a single man for other duties, so that our strength was dissolved and our momentum slackened, and we could only watch helplessly as the lawless were left alone.
translations.idiomatic: Under Zhenyuan, Yan, Zhao, and Wei rebelled in Shandong while Qi and Cai rebelled in Henan. Liang, Xu, Chen, Ru, the Baima and Meng fords, Xiang, Deng, An, Huang, and Shouchun each held a dozen heavy garrisons—barely enough to guard their own prefectural seats, never sparing a single soldier for elsewhere. Our force splintered, our energy drained, and we could only stand by while outlaws did as they pleased.

sentences.zh: 階此，蜀亦叛，吳亦叛，其他未叛者，迎時上下，不可保信。

translations.literal: Following upon this, Shu also rebelled, Wu also rebelled; among those not yet in rebellion, all shifted with the times—none could be trusted.
translations.idiomatic: On that foundation Shu rose in revolt, then Wu; even those who had not yet rebelled swayed with every shift of fortune, and no loyalty could be counted on.

sentences.zh: 自元和初至今二十九年間，得蜀，得吳，得蔡，得齊，收郡縣二百餘城，所未能得，唯山東百城耳。

translations.literal: From the beginning of Yuanhe to the present, twenty-nine years: we have taken Shu, taken Wu, taken Cai, taken Qi, recovered more than two hundred prefectures and counties; what we have not yet taken is only the hundred cities of Shandong.
translations.idiomatic: In the twenty-nine years since Yuanhe began we have won back Shu, Wu, Cai, and Qi and retaken more than two hundred commanderies and counties. Only the hundred-odd cities of Shandong still elude us.

sentences.zh: 土地人戶，財物甲兵，較之往年，豈不綽綽乎？

translations.literal: Land, households, wealth, armor, and weapons—compared with years past, are they not ample?
translations.idiomatic: Territory, population, treasure, arms, and armor—measured against former days, are we not flush with strength?

sentences.zh: 亦足自以為治也。

translations.literal: It is also enough to regard oneself as well governed.
translations.idiomatic: By those measures alone one might call the realm well ordered.

sentences.zh: 法令制度，品式條章，果自治乎？

translations.literal: Laws, ordinances, institutions, grades, forms, and statutes—are they truly self-governed?
translations.idiomatic: Do our laws, ranks, regulations, and statutes truly answer to the throne, or to local strongmen?

sentences.zh: 賢才奸惡，搜選置舍，果自治乎？

translations.literal: The worthy and the wicked, search, selection, placement, and lodging—are they truly self-governed?
translations.idiomatic: Are the appointment and dismissal of the worthy and the wicked truly in the court's hands?

sentences.zh: 障戍鎮守，干戈車馬，果自治乎？

translations.literal: Barrier garrisons, frontier defense, spears, chariots, and horses—are they truly self-governed?
translations.idiomatic: Do frontier garrisons, weapons, chariots, and horses obey the center?

sentences.zh: 井閭阡陌，倉廩財賦，果自治乎？

translations.literal: Wells, lanes, fields, granaries, and revenue—are they truly self-governed?
translations.idiomatic: Do fields, villages, granaries, and tax grain flow to the capital as they should?

sentences.zh: 如不果自治，是助虜為虜。

translations.literal: If they are not truly self-governed, this is helping the foe to be foe.
translations.idiomatic: If the answer is no, we are arming our enemies to act as enemies.

sentences.zh: 環土三千里，植根七十年，復有天下陰為之助，則安可以取？

translations.literal: Three thousand li of encircling territory, roots planted seventy years, and again the realm's hidden forces aiding them—how then may they be taken?
translations.idiomatic: Three thousand li of entrenched soil, seventy years of deep roots, and half the empire secretly abetting them—how could such ground be seized by force alone?

sentences.zh: 故曰：上策莫如自治。

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: the highest policy is none like self-governance.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the supreme strategy: put the realm in order at home.

sentences.zh: 中策莫如取魏。

translations.literal: The middle policy is none like taking Wei.
translations.idiomatic: The second-best strategy: secure Wei.

sentences.zh: 魏於山東最重，於河南亦最重。

translations.literal: Wei is weightiest in Shandong and also weightiest in Henan.
translations.idiomatic: Wei holds the greatest weight in Shandong and the greatest weight in Henan alike.

sentences.zh: 魏在山東，以其能遮趙也。

translations.literal: Wei in Shandong—because it can screen off Zhao.
translations.idiomatic: In Shandong, Wei matters because it blocks Zhao.

sentences.zh: 既不可越魏以取趙，固不可越趙以取燕。

translations.literal: Since one cannot cross Wei to take Zhao, solidly one cannot cross Zhao to take Yan.
translations.idiomatic: You cannot march past Wei to strike Zhao, nor past Zhao to strike Yan.

sentences.zh: 是燕、趙常取重於魏，魏常操燕、趙之命。

translations.literal: Thus Yan and Zhao constantly take their weight from Wei; Wei constantly holds Yan and Zhao's command.
translations.idiomatic: Yan and Zhao therefore depend on Wei for leverage, and Wei holds their fate in its hands.

sentences.zh: 故魏在山東最重。

translations.literal: Therefore Wei is weightiest in Shandong.
translations.idiomatic: That is why Wei is paramount in Shandong.

sentences.zh: 黎陽距白馬津三十里，新鄉距盟津一百五十里，陴壘相望，朝駕暮戰，是二津，虜能潰一，則馳入成臯，不數日間。

translations.literal: Liyang is thirty li from Baima Ford, Xinxiang one hundred fifty li from Meng Ford; ramparts face each other, battle by morning and evening—these two fords, if the foe can breach one, they gallop into Chenggao within a few days.
translations.idiomatic: Liyang lies thirty li from Baima Ford, Xinxiang a hundred fifty li from Meng Ford. Fortresses stare across at one another; armies fight at dawn and dusk. If the enemy breaks either ford, they ride into Chenggao within days.

sentences.zh: 故魏於河南亦最重。

translations.literal: Therefore Wei is also weightiest in Henan.
translations.idiomatic: For the same reason Wei is paramount in Henan.

sentences.zh: 元和中，舉天下兵誅蔡，誅齊，頓之五年，無山東憂者，以能得魏也。

translations.literal: In the Yuanhe era, the empire raised its armies to punish Cai and punish Qi; halted five years with no Shandong worry—because it could obtain Wei.
translations.idiomatic: Under Yuanhe the court mobilized the realm against Cai and Qi. For five years Shandong gave no trouble—because Wei was won.

sentences.zh: 昨日誅滄，頓之三年，無山東憂，亦以能得魏也。

translations.literal: Yesterday Cang was punished; halted three years with no Shandong worry—also because it could obtain Wei.
translations.idiomatic: When Cangzhou was crushed recently, Shandong stayed quiet for three years—for the same reason: Wei was held.

sentences.zh: 長慶初誅趙，一日五諸侯兵四出潰解，以失魏也。

translations.literal: In the early Changqing era Zhao was punished; in one day the five feudatories' armies marched out on four sides and collapsed in rout—because Wei was lost.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Changqing, when Zhao was attacked, the five allied commands marched out and shattered in a single day—because Wei had been lost.

sentences.zh: 昨日誅趙，罷如長慶時，亦以失魏也。

translations.literal: Yesterday Zhao was punished; the halt was like Changqing—also because Wei was lost.
translations.idiomatic: The recent campaign against Zhao stalled as at Changqing—for the same reason: Wei was lost.

sentences.zh: 故河南、山東之輕重在魏。

translations.literal: Therefore the weight of Henan and Shandong lies in Wei.
translations.idiomatic: The balance of Henan and Shandong therefore turns on Wei.

sentences.zh: 非魏強大，地形使然也。

translations.literal: It is not that Wei is strong and great—the terrain makes it so.
translations.idiomatic: This is not because Wei is mighty in itself, but because geography makes it so.

sentences.zh: 故曰：取魏為中策。

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: taking Wei is the middle policy.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the middle strategy: take Wei.

sentences.zh: 最下策為浪戰，不計地勢，不審攻守是也。

translations.literal: The lowest policy is reckless warfare—not calculating terrain, not examining attack and defense.
translations.idiomatic: The worst strategy is reckless war: ignoring terrain and misjudging when to strike or hold.

sentences.zh: 兵多粟多，驅人使戰者，便於守；

translations.literal: Many troops and much grain, driving men to fight—this favors defense.
translations.idiomatic: Abundant troops and grain, with soldiers driven to battle, favor the defender.

sentences.zh: 兵少粟少，人不驅自戰者，便於戰。

translations.literal: Few troops and little grain, men fighting without being driven—this favors attack.
translations.idiomatic: Few troops and little grain, with men who fight of their own will, favor the attacker.

sentences.zh: 故我常失於戰，虜常困於守。

translations.literal: Therefore we constantly lose in battle; the foe is constantly trapped in defense.
translations.idiomatic: We therefore keep losing in open battle while the enemy keeps winning behind walls.

sentences.zh: 山東叛且三五世，後生所見言語舉止，無非叛也，以為事理正當如此，沈酣入骨髓，無以為非者，至有圍急食盡，啖屍以戰。

translations.literal: Shandong has rebelled for three or five generations; what the young have seen in speech and conduct is nothing but rebellion, taking it as reason and right, sunk into the marrow with none to call it wrong—even when besieged to the end of food, eating corpses to fight.
translations.idiomatic: Shandong has been in revolt for three to five generations. The young know no speech or gesture but treason; they take rebellion for the natural order, steeped to the bone, with none to call it shame—even eating the dead when sieges leave them starving.

sentences.zh: 以此為俗，豈可與決一勝一負哉？

translations.literal: With this as custom, how may one with them decide one victory or one defeat?
translations.idiomatic: Where such ways are custom, how can a single pitched battle settle the matter?

sentences.zh: 自十餘年凡三收趙，食盡且下。

translations.literal: In more than ten years Zhao has been taken three times, food exhausted and on the verge of fall.
translations.idiomatic: In little more than a decade we have thrice brought Zhao to starvation's edge.

sentences.zh: 郗士美敗，趙復振；

translations.literal: Xi Shimei was defeated, and Zhao revived.
translations.idiomatic: When Xi Shimei was beaten, Zhao rose again.

sentences.zh: 杜叔良敗，趙復振；

translations.literal: Du Shuliang was defeated, and Zhao revived.
translations.idiomatic: When Du Shuliang was beaten, Zhao rose again.

sentences.zh: 李聽敗，趙復振。

translations.literal: Li Ting was defeated, and Zhao revived.
translations.idiomatic: When Li Ting was beaten, Zhao rose again.

sentences.zh: 故曰：不計地勢，不審攻守，為浪戰，最下策也。

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: not calculating terrain, not examining attack and defense, is reckless warfare—the lowest policy.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the verdict: to ignore terrain and misjudge attack and defense is reckless war—the worst of strategies.

sentences.zh: 累遷左補闕、史館修撰，改膳部員外郎。

translations.literal: He was repeatedly promoted to Left Remonstrator and Historiographical Compiler, then changed to Vice Director of the Board of Rites.
translations.idiomatic: He rose through Left Remonstrator and historiographical compiler to Vice Director of the Board of Rites.

sentences.zh: 宰相李德裕素奇其才。

translations.literal: Chief Minister Li Deyu had long marveled at his talent.
translations.idiomatic: Chief Minister Li Deyu had long prized his ability.

sentences.zh: 會昌中，黠戛斯破回鶻，回鶻種落潰入漠南，牧說德裕不如遂取之，以為：「兩漢伐虜，常以秋冬，當匈奴勁弓折膠，重馬免乳，與之相校，故敗多勝少。

translations.literal: In the Huichang era the Kirghiz destroyed the Uyghurs, and Uyghur clans fled in rout into the desert south. Mu urged Deyu that it would be better to seize the moment and take them, reasoning: "The two Han dynasties campaigned against the northern barbarians always in autumn and winter, when the Xiongnu bows lost their glue and heavy mares ceased nursing—measured against them, defeats were many and victories few.
translations.idiomatic: During Huichang the Kirghiz shattered the Uyghurs, and Uyghur tribes poured into the southern steppe. Mu urged Deyu to strike at once: "Han campaigns against the northern tribes usually came in autumn and winter, when Xiongnu bows stiffened and brood mares dried up—against such seasons our forebears won few battles.

sentences.zh: 今若以仲夏發幽、并突騎及酒泉兵，出其意外，一舉無類矣。」

translations.literal: Now if in midsummer we send Youzhou and Bingzhou shock cavalry with Jiuquan troops, striking where they do not expect it, in one blow none would remain.
translations.idiomatic: Send Youzhou and Bingzhou shock cavalry now, in midsummer, with Jiuquan troops, and catch them unprepared—one stroke could wipe them out.

sentences.zh: 德裕善之。

translations.literal: Deyu approved of it.
translations.idiomatic: Deyu approved the plan.

sentences.zh: 會劉稹拒命，詔諸鎮兵討之，牧復移書於德裕，以「河陽西北去天井關強百里，用萬人為壘，窒其口，深壁勿與戰。

translations.literal: When Liu Zhen defied orders and edicts went out for the feudatories to campaign against him, Mu again wrote to Deyu that "northwest of Heyang to Tianjing Pass is a hundred li of strong ground; with ten thousand men as a barrier, choke the pass and deepen the walls without giving battle.
translations.idiomatic: When Liu Zhen rebelled and the court ordered the circuits to march, Mu wrote again to Deyu: "A hundred li northwest of Heyang lies Tianjing Pass. Ten thousand men could fortify it, seal the gap, and refuse battle.

sentences.zh: 成德軍世與昭義為敵，王元逵思一雪以自奮，然不能長驅徑搗上黨，其必取者在西面。

translations.literal: The Chengde army has long been enemy to Zhaoyi; Wang Yuankui longs to wipe away shame in one stroke and exert himself, yet he cannot drive straight to strike Shangdang—the ground he must take lies on the west.
translations.idiomatic: Chengde and Zhaoyi have been enemies for generations. Wang Yuankui burns to redeem his honor in one thrust, yet he cannot plunge straight at Shangdang—his road lies on the western flank.

sentences.zh: 今若以忠武、武寧兩軍益青州精甲五千、宣潤弩手二千，道絳而入，不數月必覆賊巢。

translations.literal: Now if with Zhongwu and Wuning two armies one adds five thousand elite armor from Qingzhou and two thousand crossbowmen from Xuan and Run, entering by way of Jiang, in not many months the rebels' nest will surely be overturned.
translations.idiomatic: Add five thousand Qingzhou armored troops and two thousand crossbowmen from Xuan and Run to the Zhongwu and Wuning armies, march through Jiangzhou, and within months the nest will fall.

sentences.zh: 昭義之食，盡仰山東，常日節度使率留食邢州，山西兵單少，可乘虛襲取。

translations.literal: Zhaoyi's food wholly depends on Shandong; on ordinary days the military commissioner keeps provisions at Xingzhou, while Shanxi troops are few—one may take advantage of emptiness and strike.
translations.idiomatic: Zhaoyi lives on grain from Shandong; its commissioner usually hoards food at Xingzhou while Shanxi is thinly garrisoned—strike the empty belly.

sentences.zh: 故兵聞拙速，未睹巧之久也」。

translations.literal: Therefore in warfare one has heard of clumsy speed, but not seen cleverness prolonged."
translations.idiomatic: In war, as the saying goes, a clumsy rush beats a clever delay."

sentences.zh: 俄而澤潞平，略如牧策。

translations.literal: Before long Ze and Lu were pacified, broadly as Mu had strategized.
translations.idiomatic: Soon Ze and Lu were pacified, much as Mu had foretold.

sentences.zh: 歷黃、池、睦三州刺史，入為司勛員外郎，常兼史職。

translations.literal: He served in succession as prefect of Huang, Chi, and Mu, entered as Vice Director of the Board of Revenue, and regularly doubled as historiographer.
translations.idiomatic: He governed Huang, Chi, and Mu in turn, then entered court as Vice Director of the Board of Revenue, usually doubling as historiographer.

sentences.zh: 改吏部，復乞為湖州刺史。

translations.literal: He was changed to the Board of Civil Office, then again begged to be prefect of Huzhou.
translations.idiomatic: He moved to the Board of Civil Office, then petitioned again to serve as prefect of Huzhou.

sentences.zh: 逾年，以考功郎中知制誥，遷中書舍人。

translations.literal: After more than a year, as Director of the Bureau of Merit he knew drafting of edicts, and was promoted to Secretariat Drafter.
translations.idiomatic: A year later, as Director of the Bureau of Merit with charge of edicts, he was promoted Secretariat Drafter.

sentences.zh: 牧剛直有奇節，不為齪齪小謹，敢論列大事，指陳病利尤切至。

translations.literal: Mu was upright with a singular integrity, not petty in small cautions, daring to debate great affairs; his pointing out of ills and benefits was especially incisive.
translations.idiomatic: Mu was blunt and unbending, careless of small proprieties, bold on great matters, and piercing when he laid out harm and profit.

sentences.zh: 少與李甘、李中敏、宋元阝善，其通古今，善處成敗，甘等不及也。

translations.literal: In youth he was friendly with Li Gan, Li Zhongmin, and Yuan Ying; in penetrating antiquity and present and handling success and failure, Gan and the others did not reach him.
translations.idiomatic: In youth he befriended Li Gan, Li Zhongmin, and Yuan Ying. None matched his grasp of past and present or his reading of rise and fall.

sentences.zh: 牧亦以疏直，時無右援者。

translations.literal: Mu also, because of his bluntness, at the time had no powerful support.
translations.idiomatic: His very bluntness left him without powerful patrons at court.

sentences.zh: 從兄悰更歷將相，而牧困躓不自振，頗怏怏不平。

translations.literal: His cousin Cong rose through general and chancellor, while Mu, frustrated and unable to lift himself, was quite resentful and uneasy.
translations.idiomatic: His cousin Cong climbed to general and chancellor while Mu, stalled and unable to rise, nursed a bitter unease.

sentences.zh: 卒，年五十。

translations.literal: He died at age fifty.
translations.idiomatic: He died at fifty.

sentences.zh: 初，牧夢人告曰：「爾應名畢。」

translations.literal: Earlier Mu dreamed a man told him: "Your allotted name is finished.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier he dreamed a voice saying, "Your destined name is spent.

sentences.zh: 復夢書「皎皎白駒」字，或曰「過隙也」。

translations.literal: Again he dreamed the writing "Bright bright the white colt," and someone said "a passing gap."
translations.idiomatic: He dreamed next the words "Bright bright the white colt," and someone said it meant "a fleeting span."

sentences.zh: 俄而炊甑裂，牧曰：「不祥也。」

translations.literal: Soon the rice steamer cracked. Mu said: "This is ill-omened.
translations.idiomatic: Soon his rice pot split. Mu said, "An ill omen.

sentences.zh: 乃自為墓誌，悉取所為文章焚之。

translations.literal: Thereupon he himself composed his epitaph and burned all the writings he had made.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote his own epitaph and burned every piece he had written.

sentences.zh: 牧於詩，情致豪邁，人號為「小杜」，以別杜甫云。

translations.literal: In poetry Mu's feeling was bold and expansive; men called him "Little Du" to distinguish him from Du Fu.
translations.idiomatic: In verse his passion ran bold and high; posterity called him "Little Du" to set him apart from Du Fu.

sentences.zh: 牧弟 顗顗，字勝之，幼病目，母禁其為學。

translations.literal: Mu's younger brother Yi, styled Shengzhi, was blind in one eye from childhood; his mother forbade his studies.
translations.idiomatic: Mu's younger brother Yi, styled Shengzhi, had been half-blind since childhood; his mother barred him from books.

sentences.zh: 舉進士，禮部侍郎賈餗語人曰：「得杜顗足敵數百人。」

translations.literal: He passed the jinshi examination. Vice Director of Rites Jia Su told others: "To obtain Du Yi is worth several hundred men.
translations.idiomatic: He took the jinshi degree. Vice Director of Rites Jia Su said, "One Du Yi is worth hundreds of candidates.

sentences.zh: 授秘書省正字。

translations.literal: He was appointed Rectifier in the Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: He was made Secretariat Rectifier.

sentences.zh: 李德裕奏為浙西府賓佐。

translations.literal: Li Deyu memorialized him as a guest officer of the Zhexi headquarters.
translations.idiomatic: Li Deyu appointed him staff officer in Zhexi.

sentences.zh: 德裕貴盛，賓客無敢忤，惟顗數諫正之。

translations.literal: When Deyu was noble and flourishing, guests did not dare contradict him; only Yi several times remonstrated and corrected him.
translations.idiomatic: At the height of Deyu's power no guest dared oppose him—only Yi spoke up again and again.

sentences.zh: 及謫袁州，嘆曰：「門下愛我皆如顗，吾無今日。」

translations.literal: When he was demoted to Yuanzhou, he sighed: "If all my retainers had loved me as Yi, I would not be here today.
translations.idiomatic: Demoted to Yuanzhou, he sighed, "Had every man under my roof advised me like Yi, I would not stand here ruined.

sentences.zh: 太和末，召為咸陽尉，直史館。

translations.literal: At the end of Taihe he was summoned as magistrate of Xianyang and served in the Historiographical Institute.
translations.idiomatic: Late in Taihe he was recalled as magistrate of Xianyang and attached to the Historiographical Institute.

sentences.zh: 常語人曰：「李訓、鄭註必敗。」

translations.literal: He often told others: "Li Xun and Zheng Zhu are certain to fail.
translations.idiomatic: He often warned, "Li Xun and Zheng Zhu are doomed to fall.

sentences.zh: 行未及都，聞難作，疏辭疾歸。

translations.literal: He had not yet reached the capital when he heard trouble had broken out; he submitted a memorial pleading illness and returned.
translations.idiomatic: Before he reached the capital the Sweet Dew coup erupted; he pleaded illness and turned back.

sentences.zh: 顗亦善屬文，與牧相上下。

translations.literal: Yi was also skilled at literary composition, nearly matching Mu.
translations.idiomatic: Yi wrote nearly as well as Mu.

sentences.zh: 竟以喪明卒。

translations.literal: In the end he died from loss of sight.
translations.idiomatic: He died at last of blindness.

sentences.zh: =令狐楚=

translations.literal: Linghu Chu
translations.idiomatic: Linghu Chu

sentences.zh: 令狐楚，字殼士，德棻之裔也。

translations.literal: Linghu Chu, styled Keshi, was a descendant of Linghu Defen.
translations.idiomatic: Linghu Chu, styled Keshi, traced his line to Linghu Defen.

sentences.zh: 生五歲，能為辭章。

translations.literal: At five years he could compose literary pieces.
translations.idiomatic: At five he could already write polished prose.

sentences.zh: 逮冠，貢進士，京兆尹將薦為第一，時許正倫輕薄士，有名長安間，能作蜚語，楚嫌其爭，讓而下之。

translations.literal: On reaching cap, he presented himself for the jinshi. The capital intendant wished to recommend him first; at the time Xu Zhenglun, a frivolous scholar with a name in Chang'an who could make slanderous talk, Chu disliked the contention and yielded, placing himself below.
translations.idiomatic: At his capping he sat for the jinshi. The capital intendant meant to rank him first, but Xu Zhenglun—a flashy man famous in Chang'an for poisonous gossip—wanted the honor. Chu disliked the quarrel and stood down.

sentences.zh: 既及第，桂管觀察使王拱愛其材，將辟楚，懼不至，乃先奏而後聘。

translations.literal: After passing, Guiguan surveillance commissioner Wang Gong loved his talent and was about to recruit Chu; fearing he would not come, he memorialized first and then sent the invitation.
translations.idiomatic: After he passed, Guiguan commissioner Wang Gong, admiring his talent, meant to hire him. Fearful Chu would refuse, Gong memorialized the court before issuing the summons.

sentences.zh: 雖在拱所，以父官并州不得奉養，未嘗豫宴樂。

translations.literal: Though in Gong's employ, because his father's office was at Bingzhou he could not support his parents and never took part in banquets or music.
translations.idiomatic: Even under Gong he would not feast or make merry, for his father served at Bingzhou and he could not attend his parents.

sentences.zh: 滿歲謝歸。

translations.literal: When his term was full he thanked and returned.
translations.idiomatic: When his tour ended he went home.

sentences.zh: 李說、嚴綬、鄭儋繼領太原，高其行，引在幕府，由掌書記至判官。

translations.literal: Li Shuo, Yan Shou, and Zheng Dan in succession held Taiyuan, admired his conduct, and brought him into their staffs, from chief secretary to administrative aide.
translations.idiomatic: Li Shuo, Yan Shou, and Zheng Dan, each in turn governing Taiyuan, prized his character and drew him into staff service—from chief secretary to administrative aide.

sentences.zh: 德宗喜文，每省太原奏，必能辨楚所為，數稱之。

translations.literal: Emperor Dezong loved literature; whenever he reviewed Taiyuan memorials he could always tell which were Chu's and repeatedly praised them.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Dezong loved letters. In every Taiyuan memorial he could pick out Chu's hand and praised it again and again.

sentences.zh: 儋暴死，不及占後事，軍大歡，將為亂。

translations.literal: Dan died violently before he could draft the posthumous memorial; the army rejoiced greatly and was about to mutiny.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Dan died suddenly before the mourning memorial was written. The army erupted in joy and neared mutiny.

sentences.zh: 夜十數騎挺刃邀取楚，使草遺奏，諸將圜視，楚色不變，秉筆輒就，以遍示，士皆感泣，一軍乃安。

translations.literal: At night a dozen horsemen with drawn blades seized Chu and made him draft the final memorial; the generals ringed round watching. Chu's color did not change; he took the brush and finished at once. When it was shown all around, the soldiers wept, and the whole army was settled.
translations.idiomatic: That night a dozen horsemen with naked blades dragged Chu out and ordered him to write the last memorial while the generals ringed him. His face never changed; he wrote at a stroke. When the text was read aloud the men wept, and the army quieted.

sentences.zh: 由是名益重。

translations.literal: From this his fame grew heavier still.
translations.idiomatic: His fame rose sharply from that hour.

sentences.zh: 以親喪解，既除，召授右拾遺。

translations.literal: He resigned on account of mourning for a parent; after the mourning period he was summoned and appointed Right Remonstrator.
translations.idiomatic: Parental mourning took him from office; when it ended he was recalled as Right Remonstrator.

sentences.zh: 憲宗時，累擢職方員外郎，知制誥。

translations.literal: Under Emperor Xianzong he was repeatedly promoted to Vice Director of the Board of War with charge of drafting edicts.
translations.idiomatic: Under Xianzong he rose to Vice Director of the Board of War with charge of edicts.

sentences.zh: 其為文，於箋奏制令尤善，每一篇成，人皆傳諷。

translations.literal: In his writing, in memorials, reports, and edicts he was especially good; whenever a piece was finished, people passed it about reciting it.
translations.idiomatic: He excelled at memorials, reports, and edicts; each finished piece was copied and recited through the capital.

sentences.zh: 皇甫镈以言利幸，與楚、蕭俛皆厚善，故薦於帝。

translations.literal: Huangfu Bo, through talk of profit, won favor; with Chu and Xiao Mian he was thickly friendly, and therefore recommended them to the emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Huangfu Bo won the throne by promising profit. He was close to Chu and Xiao Mian and pushed them forward.

sentences.zh: 帝亦自聞其名，召為翰林學士，進中書舍人。

translations.literal: The emperor also himself had heard his name and summoned him as Hanlin Academician, promoting him to Secretariat Drafter.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor had heard his name and summoned him to the Hanlin, then promoted him Secretariat Drafter.

sentences.zh: 方伐蔡，久未下，議者多欲罷兵，帝獨與裴度不肯赦。

translations.literal: When they were campaigning against Cai it was long without success; many in council wished to cease the army, but the emperor alone with Pei Du refused to pardon.
translations.idiomatic: The war on Cai dragged on; many at court urged withdrawal, but the emperor and Pei Du alone refused to relent.

sentences.zh: 元和十二年，度以宰相領彰義節度使，楚草制，其辭有所不合，度得其情。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year of Yuanhe, Du, as chancellor, also held Zhangyi as military commissioner. Chu drafted the edict; its wording did not accord. Du grasped his intent.
translations.idiomatic: In Yuanhe twelve Du served as chancellor and Zhangyi commissioner. Chu drafted the commission; the wording betrayed his mind, and Du saw it.

sentences.zh: 時宰相李逢吉與楚善，皆不助度，故帝罷逢吉，停楚學士，但為中書舍人。

translations.literal: At the time Chief Minister Li Fengji was friendly with Chu; both did not aid Du, so the emperor dismissed Fengji and suspended Chu as academician, leaving him only Secretariat Drafter.
translations.idiomatic: Chief Minister Li Fengji favored Chu; neither helped Du. The emperor removed Fengji and stripped Chu of his Hanlin post, leaving him drafter only.

sentences.zh: 俄出為華州刺史。

translations.literal: Before long he went out as prefect of Huazhou.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was sent out as prefect of Huazhou.

sentences.zh: 後它學士比比宣事不切旨，帝抵其草，思楚之才。

translations.literal: Later other academicians in succession announced affairs not to the emperor's intent; the emperor struck their drafts and thought of Chu's talent.
translations.idiomatic: Later academicians repeatedly missed the emperor's meaning; he threw down their drafts and remembered Chu's pen.

sentences.zh: 镈既相，擢楚河陽懷節度使，代烏重胤。

translations.literal: After Bo became chancellor, he promoted Chu to military commissioner of Heyang and Huaizhou, replacing Wu Chongyin.
translations.idiomatic: Once Bo became chancellor he made Chu military commissioner of Heyang and Huaizhou, replacing Wu Chongyin.

sentences.zh: 始，重胤徙滄州，以河陽士三千從，士不樂，半道潰歸，保北城，將轉掠旁州。

translations.literal: At the start, when Chongyin was transferred to Cangzhou, three thousand Heyang soldiers followed him; the troops were displeased, and halfway they broke away and returned, holding the north city and about to turn to plunder neighboring prefectures.
translations.idiomatic: When Chongyin was moved to Cangzhou three thousand Heyang men marched with him. Unhappy, half the force deserted midway, seized the north wall, and prepared to raid neighboring prefectures.

sentences.zh: 楚至中潬，以數騎自往勞之。

translations.literal: Chu reached Zhongtan and with a few horsemen went himself to comfort them.
translations.idiomatic: Chu reached Zhongtan and rode out alone with a handful of escorts to face them.

sentences.zh: 眾甲而出，見楚不疑，乃皆降。

translations.literal: The masses came out in armor and, seeing Chu without suspicion, all surrendered.
translations.idiomatic: They came out armed, saw he did not flinch, and laid down their weapons.

sentences.zh: 楚斬其首惡，眾遂定。

translations.literal: Chu beheaded the chief ringleaders, and the masses were then settled.
translations.idiomatic: Chu executed the ringleaders and the troops quieted.

sentences.zh: 度出太原，镈薦楚為中書侍郎、同中書門下平章事。

translations.literal: When Du left Taiyuan, Bo recommended Chu as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Associate Grand Councilor of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
translations.idiomatic: When Du left Taiyuan, Bo recommended Chu as Vice Director of the Secretariat and associate grand councilor.

sentences.zh: 穆宗即位，進門下侍郎。

translations.literal: When Muzong took the throne, [Chu] was advanced to Vice Director of the Chancellery.
translations.idiomatic: On Muzong's accession, Linghu Chu was promoted to Vice Director of the Chancellery.

sentences.zh: 镈得罪，時謂楚緣镈以進，且嘗逐裴度，天下所共疾，會蕭俛輔政，乃不敢言。

translations.literal: Bo fell from favor; at the time it was said Chu had advanced by riding on Bo, and moreover had once driven out Pei Du—what all under Heaven jointly detested. When Xiao Fu came to assist in government, none dared speak of it.
translations.idiomatic: When Duan Bo fell, many said Chu had climbed on his patron's back and had once hounded Pei Du from office—crimes the empire shared in loathing. Xiao Fu now held the reins, and for a time the court held its tongue.

sentences.zh: 方營景陵，詔楚為使，而親吏韋正牧、奉天令於翚等不償傭錢十五萬緡，楚獻以為羨余，怨訴系路。

translations.literal: Just then they were building the Jing Mausoleum; the Emperor ordered Chu as commissioner. Yet his close clerks Wei Zhengyu and the Fengtian magistrate Yu Hui and others did not repay hired labor to the amount of one hundred fifty thousand strings of cash. Chu presented it as surplus revenue; complaints of grievance lined the roads.
translations.idiomatic: While the Jing Mausoleum was under construction, Chu was named commissioner. His intimates Wei Zhengyu and Fengtian magistrate Yu Hui, among others, withheld a hundred and fifty thousand strings in wages. Chu booked the sum as surplus; petitioners clogged the highways with their grievances.

sentences.zh: 詔捕翚等下獄誅，出楚為宣歙觀察使。

translations.literal: An edict ordered Yu Hui and the rest seized, imprisoned, and executed; Chu was sent out as Xuanchen surveillance commissioner.
translations.idiomatic: The throne had Yu Hui and his fellows arrested and put to death, and exiled Chu to the Xuanchen post as surveillance commissioner.

sentences.zh: 俄貶衡州刺史，再徙，以太子賓客分司東都。

translations.literal: Soon he was demoted to Hengzhou prefect; moved again; then made Honored Guest of the Heir Apparent with duty at the Eastern Capital.
translations.idiomatic: Shortly he was demoted to prefect of Hengzhou, transferred once more, and finally kept the title Honored Guest of the Heir Apparent while serving at Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 長慶二年，擢陜虢觀察使，諫官論執不置，楚至陜一日，復罷，還東都。

translations.literal: In the second year of Changqing he was raised to Shaan-Guo surveillance commissioner; remonstrating officials argued and would not let the appointment stand. Chu reached Shaan for one day, was dismissed again, and returned to the Eastern Capital.
translations.idiomatic: In Changqing year two he was named Shaan-Guo surveillance commissioner, but the remonstrators blocked the appointment. Chu reached his post for a single day, was removed, and went back to Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 會逢吉復相，力起楚，以李紳在翰林沮之，不克。

translations.literal: It happened that Fengji again became chief minister and strove to raise Chu; because Li Shen was in the Hanlin and obstructed it, he did not succeed.
translations.idiomatic: Li Fengji returned to the chancellery and pressed hard to restore Chu, but Li Shen in the Hanlin Academy stood in the way, and the effort failed.

sentences.zh: 敬宗立，逐出紳，即拜楚為河南尹。

translations.literal: When Jingzong took the throne, Shen was driven out; Chu was at once appointed Henan Intendant.
translations.idiomatic: Jingzong's accession brought Li Shen's expulsion and Chu's immediate appointment as Henan Intendant.

sentences.zh: 遷宣武節度使。

translations.literal: He was transferred to military commissioner of Xuanwu.
translations.idiomatic: He was made military commissioner of Xuanwu.

sentences.zh: 汴軍以驕故，而韓弘弟兄務以峻法繩治，士偷於安，無革心。

translations.literal: The Bian army had grown proud by custom, while Han Hong and his brothers strove to bind them with harsh law; the soldiers stole ease and had no mind to reform.
translations.idiomatic: Bianzhou's troops had long been arrogant; Han Hong and his brothers ruled them with pitiless statutes until the men clung to comfort and would not change their ways.

sentences.zh: 楚至，解去酷烈，以仁惠鐫諭，人人悅喜，遂為善俗。

translations.literal: When Chu arrived he removed the cruel severity and, with humane kindness engraved in counsel, every man rejoiced; it thus became a good custom.
translations.idiomatic: Chu lifted the harshest punishments and won the ranks with measured mercy until joy spread through the camps and decent custom took root.

sentences.zh: 入為戶部尚書，俄拜東都留守，徙天平節度使。

translations.literal: He entered court as Minister of Revenue; soon he was appointed Eastern Capital regent and transferred to military commissioner of Tianping.
translations.idiomatic: He was recalled as Minister of Revenue, soon made regent of the Eastern Capital, then transferred to Tianping as military commissioner.

sentences.zh: 始，汴、鄆帥每至，以州錢二百萬入私藏，楚獨辭不取。

translations.literal: From the first, whenever the Bian and Yan commanders arrived they put two million in prefectural funds into private stores; Chu alone declined and would not take it.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier commanders of Bian and Yan had each pocketed two million strings of prefectural revenue; Chu alone refused the custom.

sentences.zh: 又毀李師古園檻僭制者。

translations.literal: He also destroyed the garden balustrades and other usurping structures of Li Shigu.
translations.idiomatic: He tore down Li Shigu's garden railings and other pretensions to princely splendor.

sentences.zh: 久之，徙節河東。

translations.literal: After a long while he was transferred to command Hedong.
translations.idiomatic: In time he was shifted to the Hedong command.

sentences.zh: 召為吏部尚書，檢校尚書右僕射。

translations.literal: He was summoned as Minister of the Civil Service and Acting Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
translations.idiomatic: He was recalled as Minister of the Civil Service and given the acting rank of Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 故事，檢校官重，則從其班；

translations.literal: By precedent, when an acting office was the heavier, one followed its court rank;
translations.idiomatic: Precedent held that when an acting appointment outranked one's regular post, one took the higher court precedence;

sentences.zh: 楚以吏部自有品，固辭，有詔嘉允。

translations.literal: Chu, because the Ministry of the Civil Service had its own grade, firmly declined; an edict praised and approved.
translations.idiomatic: Chu argued that the civil-service ministry carried its own proper rank and firmly declined; the throne commended his scruple.

sentences.zh: 俄兼太常卿，進拜左僕射、彭陽郡公。

translations.literal: Soon he also held the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness; he was advanced to Left Vice Director and Duke of Pengyang.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness as well, then promoted to Left Vice Director and Duke of Pengyang.

sentences.zh: 會李訓亂，將相皆系神策軍。

translations.literal: It happened that Li Xun's rebellion broke out; chief ministers and generals were all detained in the Shence Army.
translations.idiomatic: When Li Xun's plot erupted, ministers and generals alike were held in the Shence barracks.

sentences.zh: 文宗夜召楚與鄭覃入禁中，楚建言：「外有三司御史，不則大臣雜治，內仗非宰相系所也。」

translations.literal: By night Emperor Wenzong summoned Chu and Zheng Tan into the inner palace; Chu offered counsel: "Outside there are the Three Offices and the censorate; if not, let great ministers jointly try the case—the inner guard is no place to detain chief ministers.
translations.idiomatic: That night Wenzong called Chu and Zheng Tan into the palace. Chu urged: "Let the Three Offices and the censorate judge this outside the palace—or at least a bench of senior ministers. The inner guard is no jail for chancellors.

sentences.zh: 帝頷之。

translations.literal: The Emperor nodded.
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor nodded.

sentences.zh: 既草詔，以王涯、賈餗冤，指其罪不切，仇士良等怨之。

translations.literal: After the draft edict was written, because Wang Ya and Jia Su were treated as wrongfully condemned and their crimes were not described sharply enough, Qiu Shiliang and the rest resented him.
translations.idiomatic: When Chu drafted the edict he treated Wang Ya and Jia Su as men wrongfully killed and named their crimes too mildly; Qiu Shiliang and his faction turned on him.

sentences.zh: 始，帝許相楚，乃不果，更用李石，而以楚為鹽鐵轉運使。

translations.literal: At first the Emperor had promised to make Chu chief minister, but it did not come to pass; Li Shi was used instead, and Chu was made salt and iron transport commissioner.
translations.idiomatic: Wenzong had meant to name Chu chancellor, but the appointment never came; Li Shi took the post instead, and Chu was sent to oversee salt and iron transport.

sentences.zh: 先是，鄭註奏建榷茶使，王涯又議官自治園植茶，人不便，楚請廢使，如舊法，從之。

translations.literal: Earlier Zheng Zhu had memorialized to establish a tea monopoly commissioner; Wang Ya had also proposed that officials themselves manage and plant tea gardens—the people found it inconvenient. Chu requested abolishing the commissioner and returning to the old law; the throne assented.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Zhu had once proposed a tea monopoly; Wang Ya wanted officials to run government tea gardens—both schemes burdened the people. Chu persuaded the court to abolish the monopoly and restore the old rules.

sentences.zh: 元和中，出禁兵畀左右街使衛宰相入朝，至建福門。

translations.literal: In the Yuanhe era forbidden troops had been given to the left and right Street commissioners to escort chancellors into court, as far as the Jianfu Gate.
translations.idiomatic: Under Yuanhe, palace troops had been lent to the Street commissioners to escort chancellors to court as far as Jianfu Gate.

sentences.zh: 及是亂，乃罷。

translations.literal: When this turmoil came, it was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: After the upheaval that practice was ended.

sentences.zh: 楚即奏：「鎮帥初拜，必戎服屬仗詣省謁辭，本於鄭註，實為亂兆，故王璠、郭行余驅將吏蹀血京師，所宜停止。」

translations.literal: Chu at once memorialized: "When a frontier commander is first appointed he must come in military dress with arms to the ministry to pay respects and take leave—this began with Zheng Zhu and was in truth an omen of disorder. Hence Wang Fan and Guo Xingyu drove officers and clerks to trample blood through the capital; it should be stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Chu memorialized at once: "New military commissioners should not be required to appear in armor at the ministries—that custom began with Zheng Zhu and foretold chaos. Wang Fan and Guo Xingyu used it to march armed men through the capital. Let it be abolished.

sentences.zh: 詔可。

translations.literal: An edict approved.
translations.idiomatic: The edict approved.

sentences.zh: 開成元年上巳，賜群臣宴曲江。

translations.literal: On the first shangsi of the first year of Kaicheng, the Emperor bestowed a banquet on the ministers at Qujiang.
translations.idiomatic: On the Kaicheng year's shangsi festival the court feasted the ministers at Qujiang.

sentences.zh: 楚以新誅大臣，暴骸未收，怨沴感結，稱疾不出，乃請給衣衾槥櫝，以斂刑骨，順陽氣。

translations.literal: Chu, because great ministers had just been executed and their exposed corpses were not yet gathered, said that resentment and ill omens were knotted together; he claimed illness and did not attend. He then asked that clothing, shrouds, and coffins be supplied to gather the bones of those put to death, in accord with the yang breath.
translations.idiomatic: Fresh executions had left bodies unburied in the streets; Chu pleaded illness and stayed away, then asked the throne for shrouds and coffins to bury the dead and ease the season's ill air.

sentences.zh: 是時，政在宦豎，數上疏辭位，拜山南西道節度使。

translations.literal: At that time power lay with the palace eunuchs; he repeatedly submitted memorials declining office and was appointed military commissioner of Shannan West Circuit.
translations.idiomatic: Eunuchs held the government; Chu resigned again and again until he was sent out as military commissioner of Shannan West.

sentences.zh: 卒，年七十二，贈司空，謚曰文。

translations.literal: He died at seventy-two; posthumously he was made Minister of Works with the posthumous title Wen.
translations.idiomatic: He died at seventy-two and was posthumously made Minister of Works with the temple name Wen.

sentences.zh: 楚外嚴重不可犯，而中寬厚，待士有禮。

translations.literal: Outwardly Chu was stern and grave and not to be violated; inwardly he was generous and thick, treating scholars with ritual.
translations.idiomatic: He seemed forbidding in public yet was warm within, and treated men of letters with full courtesy.

sentences.zh: 客以星步鬼神進者，一不接。

translations.literal: Guests who advanced by star-stepping or spirits—he would not receive a single one.
translations.idiomatic: He would not admit a single guest who traded in astrology or ghost lore.

sentences.zh: 為政善撫禦，治有績，人人得所宜。

translations.literal: In governing he was good at soothing and controlling; his administration had achievements, and every man obtained what suited him.
translations.idiomatic: He governed with a soothing hand and left a record of real achievement; under him each man found his proper place.

sentences.zh: 疾甚，諸子進藥，不肯禦，曰：「士固有命，何事此物邪？」

translations.literal: When his illness was severe his sons presented medicine; he would not take it, saying: "A gentleman has his allotted span—what need of such things?
translations.idiomatic: As he lay dying his sons brought medicine; he refused it. "A gentleman has his allotted span," he said. "What need of this?

sentences.zh: 自力為奏謝天子，召門人李商隱曰：「吾氣魄且盡，可助我成之。」

translations.literal: By his own strength he drafted a memorial thanking the Son of Heaven and summoned his disciple Li Shangyin, saying: "My breath and spirit are nearly spent—help me finish this."
translations.idiomatic: He forced himself to draft a final memorial to the throne and called Li Shangyin: "My strength is almost gone—help me complete this."

sentences.zh: 其大要以甘露事誅譴者眾，請霽威，普見昭洗。

translations.literal: Its main point was that many had been killed and punished in the Sweet Dew affair and he asked that majesty be cleared, that all might broadly receive exoneration.
translations.idiomatic: The heart of it pleaded that the Sweet Dew purge had slain too many and begged a general amnesty to wash the realm clean.

sentences.zh: 辭致曲盡，無所謬脫。

translations.literal: The language was bent to the utmost and nowhere fell into error.
translations.idiomatic: The prose was polished to the last degree and never slipped into falsehood.

sentences.zh: 書已，敕諸子曰：「吾生無益於時，無請謚，勿求鼓吹，以布車一乘葬，銘誌無擇高位。」

translations.literal: When the writing was done he charged his sons: "In life I was of no benefit to the age—do not request a posthumous title, do not seek funeral music; bury me in a single cloth-covered cart, and let no high office be chosen for the epitaph.
translations.idiomatic: When the draft was finished he told his sons: "I did little for my time—seek no posthumous name, no funeral band; bury me in one plain cart and let no great minister write my stone.

sentences.zh: 是夕，有大星隕寢上，其光燭廷。

translations.literal: That night a great star fell on his sleeping hall; its light lit the courtyard.
translations.idiomatic: That night a great star fell on his chamber and lit the courtyard.

sentences.zh: 坐與家人訣，乃終。

translations.literal: He sat and took leave of his family, then died.
translations.idiomatic: He bade his household farewell and died.

sentences.zh: 有詔停鹵簿以申其志。

translations.literal: An edict halted the funeral escort to honor his wish.
translations.idiomatic: The throne withheld the full funeral escort to honor his wish.

sentences.zh: 子緒、綯，顯於時。

translations.literal: His sons were Xu and Tao, both prominent in their time.
translations.idiomatic: His sons Xu and Tao both rose to prominence.

sentences.zh: 子 緒緒以蔭仕，歷隋、壽、汝三州刺史，有佳政。

translations.literal: His son Xu entered office by yin privilege and served in succession as prefect of Sui, Shou, and Ru—his governance was excellent.
translations.idiomatic: His son Xu entered service by inherited privilege and governed Sui, Shou, and Ru in turn with a fine record.

sentences.zh: 汝人請刻石頌德，緒以綯當國，固讓。

translations.literal: The people of Ru asked to carve stone praising his virtue; Xu, because Tao held the state, firmly declined.
translations.idiomatic: The people of Ru wanted a stone inscription in his praise; Xu refused, not wishing to trade on his brother Tao's power at court.

sentences.zh: 宣宗嘉其意，乃止。

translations.literal: Emperor Xuanzong praised his intent and thereupon stopped it.
translations.idiomatic: Xuanzong admired his restraint and let the project die.

sentences.zh: 子 綯綯，字子直，舉進士，擢累左補闕、右司郎中。

translations.literal: His son Tao, styled Zipzhi, passed the jinshi and was repeatedly promoted to Left Suppleant Censor and Right Director in the Department of State Affairs.
translations.idiomatic: His son Tao, styled Zipzhi, took the jinshi and rose through Left Suppleant Censor to Right Director in the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 出為湖州刺史。

translations.literal: He went out as prefect of Huzhou.
translations.idiomatic: He was posted as prefect of Huzhou.

sentences.zh: 大中初，宣宗謂宰相白敏中曰：「憲宗葬，道遇風雨，六宮百官皆避，獨見頎而髯者奉梓宮不去，果誰耶？」

translations.literal: In the early Dazhong era Emperor Xuanzong said to Chief Minister Bai Minzhong: "When Xianzong was buried, the road met wind and rain; the six palaces and the hundred officials all drew aside—only a tall man with a beard was seen holding the bier and not leaving. Who was he in the end?
translations.idiomatic: Early in Dazhong, Xuanzong asked Bai Minzhong: "At Xianzong's burial a storm struck the procession. Palaces and officials alike took shelter—yet one tall, bearded man never left the bier. Who was he?

sentences.zh: 敏中言：「山陵使令狐楚。」

translations.literal: Minzhong said: "The mountain-tomb commissioner Linghu Chu."
translations.idiomatic: Minzhong answered: "The tomb commissioner Linghu Chu."

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「有子乎？」

translations.literal: The Emperor said: "Are there sons?"
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor asked whether he had any sons.

sentences.zh: 對曰：「緒少風痹，不勝用。

translations.literal: He replied: "Xu from youth has wind paralysis and cannot bear employment. Tao now holds Huzhou.
translations.idiomatic: He replied: "Xu has been crippled by wind paralysis since youth and is unfit for office. Tao now governs Huzhou.

sentences.zh: 綯今守湖州。」

translations.literal: Tao now guards Huzhou."
translations.idiomatic: Tao presently serves as prefect of Huzhou."

sentences.zh: 因曰：「其為人，宰相器也。」

translations.literal: He then said: "In his conduct he has the measure of a chief minister."
translations.idiomatic: He added: "In character he has the makings of a chancellor."

sentences.zh: 即召為考功郎中，知制誥。

translations.literal: He was at once summoned as Director in the Ministry of Personnel and put in charge of drafting edicts.
translations.idiomatic: Tao was summoned at once as Director in the Ministry of Personnel with charge of drafting edicts.

sentences.zh: 入翰林為學士。

translations.literal: He entered the Hanlin as academician.
translations.idiomatic: He entered the Hanlin Academy as academician.

sentences.zh: 它夜，召與論人間疾苦，帝出《金鏡》書曰：「太宗所著也，卿為我舉其要。」

translations.literal: On another night he was summoned to discuss the people's hardships; the Emperor brought out the book The Golden Mirror and said: "This is what Taizong wrote—expound its essentials for me.
translations.idiomatic: Another night the Emperor called him to speak of the people's hardships and produced The Golden Mirror. "Taizong wrote this," he said. "Give me its heart.

sentences.zh: 綯擿語曰：「至治未嘗任不肖，至亂未嘗任賢。

translations.literal: Tao plucked out a passage and said: "In the greatest order one never employs the unworthy; in the greatest disorder one never employs the worthy. Employ the worthy and you enjoy the fortune of all under Heaven; employ the unworthy and you suffer the calamity of all under Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Tao quoted: "Perfect order never rests on unworthy men; perfect chaos never rests on worthy men. Choose the worthy and the empire prospers; choose the unworthy and the empire falls.

sentences.zh: 任賢，享天下之福；

translations.literal: Employ the worthy and you enjoy the fortune of all under Heaven;
translations.idiomatic: Choose the worthy, and the empire prospers;

sentences.zh: 任不肖，罹天下之禍。」

translations.literal: employ the unworthy and you suffer the calamity of all under Heaven."
translations.idiomatic: choose the unworthy, and the empire falls."

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「善，朕讀此嘗三復乃已。」

translations.literal: The Emperor said: "Well said—I have read this and always turned back three times before stopping."
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor said: "Well said. I have read that passage thrice over and still return to it."

sentences.zh: 綯再拜曰：「陛下必欲興王業，舍此孰先？

translations.literal: Tao bowed again and said: "If Your Majesty truly wishes to raise a royal enterprise, apart from this what comes first?
translations.idiomatic: Tao bowed again. "If Your Majesty means to build a true kingship, where else would you begin?

sentences.zh: 《詩》曰：『惟其有之，是以似之。』」

translations.literal: The Odes say: 'Because he possesses them, therefore he is like them.'
translations.idiomatic: The Odes say: 'Because he has such men, he is like them.'

sentences.zh: 進中書舍人，襲彭陽男。

translations.literal: He was advanced to Drafting Attendant in the Secretariat and inherited the title Baron of Pengyang."
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to Drafting Attendant in the Secretariat and inherited the barony of Pengyang."

sentences.zh: 遷御史中丞，再遷兵部侍郎。

translations.literal: He was transferred to Vice Censor-in-Chief and again transferred to Vice Minister of War.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to Vice Censor-in-Chief, then to Vice Minister of War.

sentences.zh: 還為翰林承旨。

translations.literal: He returned as Hanlin Academician-in-Chief.
translations.idiomatic: He returned to the Hanlin as Academician-in-Chief.

sentences.zh: 夜對禁中，燭盡，帝以乘輿、金蓮華炬送還，院吏望見，以為天子來。

translations.literal: At night he answered in the forbidden palace; when the candles were spent the Emperor sent him back with the imperial carriage and golden lotus torches; the academy clerks saw it from afar and thought the Son of Heaven was coming.
translations.idiomatic: One night audience ran until the candles burned out; the Emperor sent him home with the imperial carriage and golden lotus torches. From a distance the Hanlin clerks thought the Son of Heaven himself was approaching.

sentences.zh: 及綯至，皆驚。

translations.literal: When Tao arrived, all were startled.
translations.idiomatic: When Tao appeared, they were all astonished.

sentences.zh: 俄同中書門下平章事，輔政十年。

translations.literal: Soon he was made Associate Chief Minister of the Secretariat-Chancellery and assisted in government for ten years.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon made Associate Chief Minister and held real power for ten years.

sentences.zh: 懿宗嗣位，由尚書左僕射、門下侍郎再拜司空。

translations.literal: When Emperor Yizong succeeded, from Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Vice Director of the Chancellery he was again appointed Minister of Works.
translations.idiomatic: At Yizong's accession he rose from Left Vice Director and Vice Director of the Chancellery to Minister of Works.

sentences.zh: 未幾，檢校司徒平章事，為河中節度使。

translations.literal: Before long, Acting Minister of Education and Associate Chief Minister, he became military commissioner of Hezhong.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was Acting Minister of Education and Associate Chief Minister, then military commissioner of Hezhong.

sentences.zh: 徙宣武，又徙淮南副大使。

translations.literal: He was transferred to Xuanwu, then again transferred to deputy ambassador of Huainan.
translations.idiomatic: He was shifted to Xuanwu, then to Huainan as deputy ambassador.

sentences.zh: 安南平，以饋運勞，封涼國公。

translations.literal: When Annan was pacified, for labor in provisioning transport he was enfeoffed as Duke of Liang.
translations.idiomatic: After the pacification of Annan he was enfeoffed Duke of Liang for his work on supply lines.

sentences.zh: 龐勛自桂州還，道浙西白沙入濁河，剽舟而上。

translations.literal: Pang Xun returned from Guizhou, entered the Zhexi White Sand into the Muddy River, and plundered boats going upstream.
translations.idiomatic: Pang Xun marched back from Guizhou, entered the Huai via Zhexi's White Sand channel, and seized boats heading upstream.

sentences.zh: 綯聞，遣使慰撫，且饋之。

translations.literal: When Tao heard of it he sent envoys to comfort and soothe them and moreover supplied them.
translations.idiomatic: Tao sent envoys to comfort the column and even furnished supplies.

sentences.zh: 裨將李湘曰：「徐兵擅還，果反矣。

translations.literal: The lieutenant general Li Xiang said: "Xuzhou soldiers left their post without leave—they will surely rebel. Though there is as yet no edict, to suppress disorder in every case I may act on my own authority.
translations.idiomatic: Lieutenant Li Xiang urged: "These Xuzhou troops left their post without orders—they mean to rebel. Even without an edict, quelling disorder is within my commission.

sentences.zh: 雖未有詔，一切制亂，我得專之。

translations.literal: Though there is as yet no edict, to suppress disorder in every case I may act on my own authority.
translations.idiomatic: Even without an edict, quelling disorder is within my commission.

sentences.zh: 今其兵不二千，而廣盤艦，張旗幟，示侈於人，其畏我甚。

translations.literal: Now their soldiers are not yet two thousand, yet they spread many ships and raise banners and flags, showing extravagance to men—they fear us greatly.
translations.idiomatic: They number fewer than two thousand yet parade a vast fleet and bright banners to overawe us—they fear us more than we fear them.

sentences.zh: 高郵厓峭水狹，若使荻曹火其前，勁兵乘其後，一舉可覆。

translations.literal: At Gaoyou the cliffs are steep and the water narrow—if we send reed boats to fire them from the front and crack troops to strike from the rear, in one move we can overturn them.
translations.idiomatic: At Gaoyou the channel narrows between steep banks. Send fire ships of reeds ahead and strike troops behind, and we can destroy them in a single blow.

sentences.zh: 不然，使得絕淮泗，合徐之不逞，禍亂滋矣。」

translations.literal: If not, let them cross the Huai and Si in force and join Xuzhou's restless elements—calamity and disorder will only grow.
